articles./blog/kolko-protein-na-den.html:
Protein is everywhere: in advertising, at the gym and on menus. But how much do you actually need? The answer depends on your weight, activity and age.

The basic recommendation for adults

The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) sets a reference intake of 0.83 g of protein per kilogram of body weight per day for healthy adults. This amount meets the needs of almost all adults who are not actively training.

For someone weighing 70 kg, that is about 58 g of protein a day.

If you exercise

The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) recommends 1.4–2.0 g/kg per day for most people who exercise regularly, especially when aiming to build muscle. For the same 70 kg person, that means about 98–140 g a day.

The ISSN advises spreading this across several meals: roughly 20–40 g of protein per meal (about 0.25–0.4 g/kg), every 3–4 hours.

After age 65

Muscles respond less strongly to protein as we age. The PROT-AGE expert group recommends 1.0–1.2 g/kg per day for healthy adults over 65, and more for active people.

A quick guide: how much for me?

WeightNot training (0.83 g/kg)Training (1.4–2.0 g/kg)
55 kg~46 g77–110 g
70 kg~58 g98–140 g
85 kg~71 g119–170 g

What that looks like on a plate

A meal with 30–45 g of protein goes a long way. The Kiwi’s menu lists approximate macros for each dish: for example, the chicken bowl has about 60 g of protein, the Caesar salad about 44 g, and the canned protein desserts about 20–22 g.

Please note: this is general information, not medical advice. If you have kidney disease, are pregnant or have a specific health condition, consult a doctor or dietitian.
articles./blog/makrosi-za-nachinaeshti.html:
Macros are the three main groups of nutrients that provide energy in food: protein, carbohydrates and fat. Understanding them helps you read both a nutrition label and a menu.

How many calories are in one gram?

Macrokcal per gramWhat it does
Protein4Muscles, fullness and recovery
Carbohydrates4Quick energy for the brain and muscles
Fat9Hormones and absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K

That is why fat adds calories fastest: a gram of fat provides more than twice the energy of a gram of protein.

A real dish as an example

The Caesar salad at Kiwi’s contains about 44 g of protein, 22 g of carbohydrates and 15 g of fat:

44 × 4 + 22 × 4 + 15 × 9 = 176 + 88 + 135 = ≈ 400 kcal

That is what the menu lists too. The calculation is never exact to the last calorie: fibre, rounding and natural variations in ingredients create small differences, so the values are approximate.

What share of calories comes from each macro?

The US Institute of Medicine gives broad ranges for adults as a share of daily calories:

  • Carbohydrates: 45–65%
  • Fat: 20–35%
  • Protein: 10–35%

The World Health Organization also recommends keeping free sugars below 10% of calories, and saturated fat below 10%.

How to use this in practice

  • Start with protein: it helps you feel full and preserve muscle during weight loss.
  • Think of calories as an overall daily budget, rather than a ban on foods.
  • Choose carbohydrate sources thoughtfully: rice, vegetables, fruit and whole grains.

Our menu lists kcal, protein, carbs and fat for every dish, making it easy to do the maths.

This is general information and does not replace advice from a doctor or dietitian.

Eating out does not have to disrupt your routine. A few simple principles can help you enjoy tasty food, feel satisfied and stay on track with your goals.

1. Build a balanced plate

Harvard’s Healthy Eating Plate offers an easy guide: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter quality protein, and a quarter whole grains or complex carbohydrates. Our protein bowls follow a similar approach: meat or fish, basmati rice and plenty of vegetables.

2. Protein first

A meal with 30+ g of protein can keep you full for longer and reduce the urge for something sweet afterwards. Chicken, turkey, fish, eggs, skyr and cottage cheese are good options.

3. Pay attention to sauces

Mayonnaise-based sauces and dressings can contain a lot of calories. Ask for sauce on the side and add as much as you need. Yoghurt-based sauces, such as those made with skyr, are lighter.

4. Drink water rather than calories

Sugary soft drinks and shakes can add 200–400 kcal to lunch. The WHO recommends keeping free sugars below 10% of daily calories, and a can of soft drink often contains more than 30 g of sugar.

5. Salt

The WHO recommends less than 5 g of salt a day for adults. Restaurant meals tend to contain more salt, so taste your food before adding any.

6. Vegetables with every meal

The WHO recommends at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day. A side salad or a bowl with plenty of vegetables can cover a substantial part of that.

7. Know what you are eating

It is easier when the restaurant tells you the nutritional values. Every dish on the Kiwi’s menu comes with approximate calories and macros.

This is general information and does not replace advice from a doctor or dietitian.

Who handles your data

Kiwi’s, 14 Nikola Karev St., Plovdiv. For questions, email kiwisplovdiv@gmail.com or call +359 892 632 470.

What data we collect

Only when you choose to subscribe: your first name, surname and email address, and the date and wording of your consent. We do not collect data about your visits.

Cookies

The site does not use advertising or tracking cookies. Your browser stores only your language choice and whether you have closed the subscription window, using localStorage; these settings are not sent to us. Fonts and images load from our server.

The map in the homepage’s Contact section is embedded from Google Maps. When it loads, Google receives your IP address and may set its own cookies under its privacy rules (policies.google.com/privacy). Kiwi’s does not have access to that data.

What we use it for

To email you news, new dishes and promotions from Kiwi’s. The legal basis is your consent under Article 6(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679. After you subscribe, we send an email with an unsubscribe link. If someone else subscribed you, that link deletes your data immediately.

How we protect it

The data is stored encrypted on our server in Bulgaria and is not shared with third parties. Only Kiwi’s has access.

How long we keep it

Until you unsubscribe. Every email from us includes an unsubscribe link, which immediately deletes your name and email address. You can also unsubscribe here or email kiwisplovdiv@gmail.com.

Your rights

You may withdraw your consent, request access to your data, or request correction or deletion at any time by emailing or calling us. You also have the right to complain to Bulgaria’s Commission for Personal Data Protection (cpdp.bg).
